question: How many entries does this memory hold, and which lines do not parse?
why: Found on the day this catalogue was created. src/doctor.mjs walked every drawer itself and counted its own unparsable lines - four hundred lines below checkIntegrity, which calls scanIntegrity for the very same walk. Two calculations of one question, in one file. The hand-rolled one was also worse advice: scanIntegrity knows the file and line of every broken entry, while the copy could only offer a grep recipe.

question: When are two entry bodies the same text?
why: Entered the day src/inbox.mjs needed body equality for replay-vs-conflict. The tempting shortcut was `a === b`, which would have called a retry differing only in line endings a CONFLICT and lost a message. Normalisation has many defensible variants (whitespace, case, CRLF, unicode); two of them in one house means two answers to 'is this the same text', and the one you believe is a coin toss.

question: How far has this memory come, so that a rollback is detectable?
why: Entered preventively. The watermark only works if exactly one recipe computes it: a second version hashing the same ids in a different order, or over a different set, would disagree with the stored mark and report a rollback that never happened. A rollback alarm that cries wolf gets switched off, and then the real rollback passes unnoticed.

question: Which drawers exist in this memory?
why: DISCARDED on the day of entry, after counting. 35 places use this idiom, and almost all of them ask something else entirely - a CLI help line listing the known types, an MCP schema enum, a dedupe command defaulting to all types. integrity.logFiles is genuinely the owner of 'which logs exist' and is already called from epoch.mjs, state.mjs and doctor.mjs; the one real second walker was fixed the same day. A latch that reports 34 innocents gets switched off, and then it stops catching the guilty too. Worth revisiting if a second enumeration ever produces a wrong number.
